html:
The Virgin of Vladimir is a Byzantine icon of the Virgin Mary holding the child Jesus, painted in Constantinople in the early 12th century and sent to Kiev around 1131. It became the most honoured icon in Russia.

It is an early example of the Eleousa or "tenderness" type, in which the child presses his cheek to his mother's face while she looks out with sorrow, as if foreseeing his death. Only the faces survive from the first painting; the rest has been repainted several times.

Prince Andrey Bogolyubsky took it from near Kiev to Vladimir in 1155, which gave it its name. In 1395 it was carried to Moscow as the army of Timur approached. Timur turned back, and the icon was credited with saving the city. It was kept in the Dormition Cathedral of the Kremlin, where tsars were crowned. It shows how Byzantine art and faith shaped Kievan Rus' and then Muscovy. It is now in the Tretyakov Gallery.
